title: Regression metrics: MSE, RMSE, MAE & R²
intro: How do you measure whether a regression model predicts well? The four standard measures — MSE, RMSE, MAE and R² — with formulas, interpretation, a fully worked car-price example, the exact closed-form formulas for the best-fit line (b1 and the y-intercept b0) and interactive plots with live metrics that show what outliers do to your metric.

blocks.html:
Training a model is step one; judging whether it is any good is step two. For that you use metrics: numbers that summarise the quality of the predictions. In regression the target \( y \) is quantitative (a number, such as a price or a temperature), so everything revolves around one question: how far are the predictions \( \hat{y} \) from the true values \( y \)?

There is a subtle difference with the loss function from the Maths & loss chapter. You use the loss during training — it must be mathematically convenient to minimise (differentiable, smooth). A metric is used afterwards to communicate how good the model is — it must be understandable to humans. Sometimes they coincide (MSE is both), sometimes not: a model trains with squared loss, but you report the MAE because it is easier to interpret.

rows: after fit(), on the test set

blocks.html: You evaluate every metric below on the test set, not on the training set. On training data the numbers can look great while the model has simply memorised the data (overfitting) — see the ML workflow.

sections.title: The three error measures: MSE, RMSE and MAE

blocks.html: The three most widely used measures for regression are the Mean Squared Error (MSE), the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) and the Mean Absolute Error (MAE). All three measure the average deviation between prediction and reality, each in its own way — and you feel that difference most when the data contains outliers.

blocks.label: Mean Squared Error
blocks.caption: Squares every error and averages: large errors count extra heavily.

blocks.label: Root Mean Squared Error
blocks.caption: The square root of the MSE — back in the same unit as the target, which makes interpretation easier.

blocks.label: Mean Absolute Error
blocks.caption: Takes the absolute error: more robust against outliers, but harder to differentiate.

blocks.html: The symbols: \( N \) is the number of data points, \( i \) is the counter over those points, \( y_i \) is the true target value of point \( i \) and \( \hat{y}_i \) ("y-hat") is the predicted target value of the model for that same point. The difference \( y_i - \hat{y}_i \) is therefore the error of a single prediction, also called the residual.

Why is the MSE more sensitive to outliers than the MAE? An error of 10 becomes \( 10^2 = 100 \) in MSE but simply 10 in MAE. One extremely wrong prediction can dominate the entire MSE — while the MAE only grows linearly with it. If your data contains a lot of noise or a few extreme points, MAE gives a fairer picture.

sections.title: Example: predicting the price of a car

blocks.html:
Consider a linear regression with three feature variables and one target variable:

  • X1 — age of the car (in years): 1, 3, 4, 7, 9
  • X2 — mileage (in 10,000 km): 5, 12, 15, 23, 30
  • X3 — number of previous owners: 1, 2, 1, 3, 2
  • Y — price of the car (in $1000): 18, 12, 10, 6, 4

After training you arrive at the parameters \( b_0 = 20 \), \( b_1 = -1 \), \( b_2 = -0.5 \) and \( b_3 = -2 \). The prediction equation is therefore:

blocks.label: car price prediction
blocks.caption: Substitute each car's feature values into the formula and you get its predicted price.

blocks.html: To judge this model you work through two steps: first the five predictions, then MSE, RMSE and MAE. The code below does exactly that and runs directly in your browser — press Run and follow the results.

blocks.caption: computing predictions and metrics
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1,  5, 1],
              [3, 12, 2],
              [4, 15, 1],
              [7, 23, 3],
              [9, 30, 2]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([18, 12, 10, 6, 4], dtype=float)
b0, b1, b2, b3 = 20.0, -1.0, -0.5, -2.0

# 1) predictions
y_hat = b0 + b1*X[:, 0] + b2*X[:, 1] + b3*X[:, 2]
print('predictions:', y_hat)

# 2) metrics
mse_value  = np.mean((y - y_hat)**2)
rmse_value = np.sqrt(mse_value)
mae_value  = np.mean(np.abs(y - y_hat))
print('MSE :', round(mse_value, 2))
print('RMSE:', round(rmse_value, 2))
print('MAE :', round(mae_value, 2))

# 3) explained variance
r2_value = 1 - np.sum((y - y_hat)**2) / np.sum((y - y.mean())**2)
print('R2  :', round(r2_value, 2), '(negative = worse than the mean!)')

blocks.html: Read the outcome like this: the average error is MAE = 6.9 ($6,900), and the RMSE comes out higher (7.79). That difference is a diagnostic signal: the five errors (3.5 / 5 / 3.5 / 10.5 / 12) are unevenly distributed — the last two cars deviate substantially and pull the squared measures up extra. If the RMSE were nearly equal to the MAE, all errors would lie close together. And note the R²: at −1.53 this model performs worse than simply predicting the mean.

This is how you implement the three measures from scratch with NumPy. Each function takes two parameters: the true target values and the predicted target values — which can come from any regression model. In practice you rarely write them yourself: scikit-learn ships mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error and r2_score ready-made, but knowing what happens inside is exactly what this site wants to convey.

blocks.caption: implementing MSE, RMSE and MAE

blocks.html: The measure that usually serves as the headline metric for regression is the explained variance, \( R^2 \). This is a statistical measure that indicates which part of the variance in the dependent variable (target) is explained by the independent variables (features). Here too you see the difference between the predicted target value \( \hat{y} \) and the mean of the actual target values \( \bar{y} \):

blocks.label: explained variance
blocks.caption: The denominator measures the spread around the mean; the numerator the spread around your predictions.

rows: the model fits every data point perfectly
no better than simply predicting the mean

blocks.html: A value close to 1 means that many data points lie close to the regression line; a value close to 0 means the line explains little. And as you saw in the car-price example: negative is possible too — then your model performs worse than a model that simply always predicts the mean. That sounds odd, but it really happens: a badly trained model, wrong features or a training set that is too small can be the cause.

blocks.caption: implementing and applying R²
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

def r2_score(y_true, y_pred):
    # numerator: spread around the predictions (model errors)
    ss_res = np.sum((y_true - y_pred)**2)
    # denominator: spread around the mean (naivest prediction)
    ss_tot = np.sum((y_true - y_true.mean())**2)
    return 1 - ss_res / ss_tot

# example values
y_true = np.array([3.0, -0.5, 2.0, 7.0])
y_pred = np.array([2.5,  0.0, 2.0, 8.0])

print('r2_score:', r2_score(y_true, y_pred))  # 0.9486081370449679

blocks.html: Compare this with the R² outcome of the car-price example: negative (−1.53). Same metric, two different worlds: here 95% of the variance is explained, there the model performs worse than the mean.

sections.title: Computing the best-fit line analytically: b1 and b0

blocks.html: So far you nudged \( b_0 \) and \( b_1 \) with sliders until the error got small. But for simple linear regression \( \hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x \) you don't have to slide at all: there are exact closed-form formulas that give the best values in one go — the values that minimise the MSE. b1 is the slope (direction coefficient) and b0 is the y-intercept: the predicted value when \( x = 0 \).

blocks.label: slope b1
blocks.caption: Divides 'how much x and y move together' by 'how much x spreads': the slope of the best-fit line.

blocks.label: y-intercept b0
blocks.caption: The best-fit line always passes through the centroid (x̄, ȳ) of the data — once you know b1, b0 follows automatically.

blocks.html:
Here \( \bar{x} \) is the mean of all x-values and \( \bar{y} \) the mean of all y-values. Read the formula for b1 like this: the numerator adds up, per point, how much x and y deviate from their means together (moving together makes it large; moving in opposite directions makes it negative). The denominator measures how much the x-values themselves spread. Small spread in x but strong co-movement gives a steep slope. The formula for b0 then forces the line exactly through the centroid \( (\bar{x}, \bar{y}) \) — drag a line through that point in an interactive plot and watch the MSE respond immediately.

Where do these formulas come from? Set the derivatives of the MSE with respect to \( b_0 \) and \( b_1 \) to zero — exactly the point where the loss landscape flattens, as in gradient descent — and solve the resulting system. For a simple line that single minimum has a closed form; gradient descent approaches the same values iteratively, while the formulas above hand them to you in one shot.

blocks.caption: computing b1 and b0 with the formulas (dataset A)
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

# dataset A — the same points as the interactive plot below
x = np.array([0.5, 1.19, 1.88, 2.58, 3.27, 3.96, 4.65, 5.35,
              6.04, 6.73, 7.42, 8.12, 8.81, 9.5])
y = np.array([3.08, 3.52, 5.83, 7.21, 6.72, 8.35, 10.45, 11.44,
              12.86, 13.6, 15.88, 17.08, 17.9, 19.78])

# means
x_mean = x.mean()
y_mean = y.mean()

# b1: co-movement of x and y, divided by the spread of x
b1 = np.sum((x - x_mean) * (y - y_mean)) / np.sum((x - x_mean)**2)

# b0: y-intercept — the line passes through (x_mean, y_mean)
b0 = y_mean - b1 * x_mean

print('b1 (slope)          :', b1)
print('b0 (y-intercept)    :', b0)

# the MSE at this pair is the smallest possible
y_hat = b0 + b1 * x
print('MSE at (b0, b1)     :', round(np.mean((y - y_hat)**2), 4))
print('R2 at (b0, b1)      :',
      round(1 - np.sum((y-y_hat)**2)/np.sum((y-y_mean)**2), 4))

blocks.html: These are exactly the values scikit-learn returns: LinearRegression stores the slope in coef_ and the y-intercept in intercept_. Go ahead and check — the code below runs in your browser and prints both side by side.

blocks.caption: checking against scikit-learn LinearRegression
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

x = np.array([0.5, 1.19, 1.88, 2.58, 3.27, 3.96, 4.65, 5.35,
              6.04, 6.73, 7.42, 8.12, 8.81, 9.5])
y = np.array([3.08, 3.52, 5.83, 7.21, 6.72, 8.35, 10.45, 11.44,
              12.86, 13.6, 15.88, 17.08, 17.9, 19.78])

model = LinearRegression().fit(x.reshape(-1, 1), y)

print('coef_      (b1):', model.coef_[0])
print('intercept_ (b0):', model.intercept_)
print('R2           :', round(model.score(x.reshape(-1, 1), y), 4))

blocks.html: With multiple features (like the car-price example: \( b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_3 x_3 \)) there is no short summation formula anymore — the computer then solves a system of equations for you (or approaches the optimum with gradient descent). If your model uses a single feature, these two formulas are the one-liner answers.

sections.title: Exploring: does the line fit the data?

blocks.html: Below are three datasets, each with one feature variable and a linear model \( y_{pred} = b_0 + b_1 x \), where \( b_0 \) is the y-intercept and \( b_1 \) the slope. Drag the sliders: every plot now has live metrics — as you drag, the MSE and \( R^2 \) are recomputed instantly and the chip lights up green once you approach the best achievable fit. Challenge yourself: first compute b1 and b0 of dataset A with the formulas above (b1 = 1.86, b0 = 1.68), then find that same pair with the sliders.

blocks.title: Dataset A — clean, linear data
blocks.subtitle: Drag b0 and b1 and watch the MSE and R² update live. Analytical optimum (formulas above): b1 = 1.86, b0 = 1.68 → MSE 0.27, R² 0.99 — the chips light up green as you get close.

blocks.title: Dataset B — with one large outlier
blocks.subtitle: One point is far off (24!). Best fit: b1 = 1.42, b0 = 5.19 → MSE 18.85. Watch the live MSE show how the squared error pulls the line towards the outlier.

blocks.title: Dataset C — curved (quadratic) data
blocks.subtitle: However you place the line: a straight line cannot fit a curve. Best straight line: b1 = 1.98, b0 = −1.83 → R² 0.82 — change the model (e.g. add x² as a feature), not just the line.

blocks.html: What these three datasets show: dataset A is the ideal case — linear, little noise, a high \( R^2 \) within reach. Dataset B shows how a single outlier inflates the squared measures (MSE/RMSE) and can shift the best line; MAE stays much less sensitive to it. Dataset C exposes the limit of the model: no straight line fits, however you slide — the solution is then not to slide better, but to pick a better model (for example \( x^2 \) as an extra feature).

With multiple features the equation becomes \( y_{pred} = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \cdots + b_n x_n \) — a plane instead of a line. The car-price example above is exactly such a case with three features.
